newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia automaker chief, wife dead in air crash.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia automaker chief, wife dead in air crash.

text.p: Yahaya Ahmad, the millionaire head of national carmaker Proton and a dominant figure in Malaysia's business world, died along with his wife and a pilot when their helicopter crashed, Yahaya's company said on Tuesday.
Yahaya, 50, his wife Rohana Othman and the pilot died Monday night in the crash near Kuala Lipis, about 250 km (155 miles) from Kuala Lumpur, a statement from DRB-Hicom Group said.
Remains of the couple and pilot Major Azlizan Abdul Manas were sent to the Kuala Terengganu hospital in east coast Terengganu state for a post-mortem, the national Bernama news agency reported.
Yahaya, whose Proton Bhd produced the ubiquitous Malaysian car, also controlled a publicly listed vehicle assembler, Diversified Resources Bhd (DRB), and heavy industrial group Hicom Holdings Bhd.
The funeral for Yahaya and his wife is scheduled for Tuesday afternoon in Marang, Terengganu, the DRB-Hicom statement said.
The two had been heading to Kuala Terengganu to visit Yahaya's sick mother, a DRB officer told Bernama. There was no immediate information on the cause of the crash, aviation authorities said.
The couple leave behind four children.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and his deputy Anwar Ibrahim, who had been a classmate of Yahaya's at Malay College Kuala Kangsar in northern Perak state, were expected to attend the funeral.

Trading in nine of Yahaya's company stocks was suspended on Tuesday following news of his death. The Kuala Lumpur stock market opened weaker on Tuesday partly on news of the Proton head's demise, dealers said.
Yahaya grabbed international headlines last year when he bought British sports car maker Group Lotus Ltd for 51 million sterling.
But even before then, he captured the imagination of the Malaysian corporate world when he engineered the 1995 privatisation of national carmaker Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd (Proton).
Anwar sought to reassure financial markets. He was quoted by Bernama as saying, "We will be committed to continue to support all the projects undertaken within the group."
Asked about a replacement for Yahaya, Anwar said, "I believe there are competent people. One major thing that he did was to ensure each division was led by competent chiefs."
Malaysian corporate leaders were stunned by Yahaya's death.
"I cancelled everything I had for today," said Tongkah Holdings Bhd chief executive officer Mokhzani Mahathir, a friend and business associate of Yahaya's.
Mokhzani, who is also a son of the prime minister, told Reuters that he and Yahaya had a "common interest in cars" and had worked on a few projects together.
"He was a great man, very humble, never forgetting where he came from and what he achieved," Mokhzani said. "He is the captain of the auto industry plus everything else."
A fund manager at a major Malaysian financial firm said: "It's a tragedy. He was very diligent in his work and had done very well."
Yahaya leaves a formidable legacy, analysts said.
The bespectacled, slight-framed automotive engineer, dubbed the "car czar" in Malaysia, virtually controlled the domestic transport business through the restructured DRB-Hicom.

Apart from the popular Proton cars, his companies controlled vehicle assemblers and a plant which turns out Malaysia's homemade motorcycle, the Kriss. His empire includes EON Bank Bhd, EON Finance Bhd and Gadek Capital Bhd His companies also run Kuala Lumpur's main bus firm.
